intro: SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 ran in three slots on 5 October: 10:00 AM, 1:30 PM and 5:00 PM. The morning and afternoon papers were mostly reported as easy to moderate or moderate, with Quant (circles, geometry, long time and work questions) and the 15-minute locked timer the main talking points. The evening paper was reported as moderate to difficult, with Quant the toughest section, and a larger candidate survey now points the same way. Reasoning was reported as easy to moderate in all three shifts, and English was dominated by voice and narration. These reviews come from candidate interviews on YouTube and a candidate survey, and all figures are unofficial.

shifts.summary: Most candidates called the morning paper easy to moderate or moderate, though a few said it felt moderate to hard because of the 15-minute lock on each section. Quant was the section where time ran short. Reasoning was lengthy for some candidates, English leaned on voice and narration, and General Awareness was easy to moderate with mostly one-line questions. A few candidates reported mouse or system lag at their centre.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Analytical reasoning had a big share (about 4–8 questions) and some of it was lengthy. There were statement-based questions, 3 addressing-type questions, 2 matrix questions and 2 syllogisms. No calendar or clock questions were reported.

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: Mostly one-line static questions across the Constitution, economy and history. About 15–16 questions were reported as doable. Current affairs was light, with only 1–2 questions.

topics.topic: Economy: the 1991 crisis, MRTP to the Competition Act 2002, Five-Year Plans
Ancient history: Pallava, Panini, Milinda Panha
Current affairs and science (Aditya L1, BIMSTEC secretariat)

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: Time was the problem. The split between Advanced Maths and arithmetic is disputed: one reviewer counted about 15–16 arithmetic and 10–11 Advanced Maths questions, while candidate interviews described the paper as mostly Advanced Maths.

topics.topic: Compound interest, percentage, profit and loss, partnership, pipes and cistern, speed-distance

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: Reported as lengthy. Voice and narration had a large share (about 7–8 questions). There were 2 sentence-rearrangement (PQRS) questions, 4 reading-comprehension questions and a cloze test. Vocabulary was from previous-year words.

asked.q: Questions on Articles 52, 170, 177 and 200 of the Constitution (as recalled by candidates).
A question on the 1991 balance of payments crisis and the role of the IMF and World Bank.
A question on the law that replaced the MRTP Act (the Competition Act, 2002).
A question on which country's model the Five-Year Plans were taken from.
A question on Aditya L1.
A question on where the BIMSTEC secretariat is located (Dhaka).
Questions on the Pallava dynasty, Panini and the Milinda Panha.
A question on the Hornbill festival.
A question on Section 20 of the BNS.
A question on the Kandla and Paradip ports.
A question on the Indian Ocean Dipole.
Circle and trigonometry questions, 2 time and work questions, and a mix of prism, cone and cylinder mensuration.

observations: Quant is where the timer hurt most: time lost on long questions cannot be recovered after the 15-minute lock.
A few candidates reported mouse-click or system lag, and some scrolling problems. These are centre-level reports.

A candidate survey (498 responses) reported an average of about 86 attempts and an average score near 141. 63% said the paper was about the same as last year, 24% said more difficult and 12% said easier. The sample is self-selected.
disagreements: Overall difficulty: most candidates said easy to moderate or moderate, while a few called it moderate to hard because of the sectional timer.
Quant mix: one reviewer said mostly arithmetic, while candidate interviews said mostly Advanced Maths.
Attempts: individual candidates reported anything from 72 to 91 attempts, so there is no single good-attempts figure.

shifts.summary: The afternoon paper was reported as easy to moderate by most candidate interviews and as moderate by others, while the survey leaned difficult. Quant was heavy on Advanced Maths, with several circle questions, and the sectional timer cut into attempts. Reasoning had some confusing statement-based questions. General Awareness was easy to moderate with very little current affairs, and English had a long reading passage early on. One centre reported a system shutdown, with the timer resuming afterwards.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Some statement-based questions confused candidates, and a blood relation question with 4 statements was skipped by many. There were 2–3 matrix questions and 1 seating question.

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: Mixed static GK with very little current affairs. Reports on the polity and economy share conflict. Science had about 2–3 biology questions and 1 physics question.

topics.topic: Sports (Asian Games, Grand Slam), Nobel, an index ranking

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: Heavy on Advanced Maths and lengthy. Circles had 4–5 questions. No Data Interpretation or statistics was reported. Candidates said the 15-minute lock cut their attempts.

topics.topic: Percentage, profit and loss, commission, partnership

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: A lengthy unseen passage came early. There were 3 sentence-rearrangement (PQRS) questions, voice and narration, a cloze test with clause identification and the idiom 'dark horse'. Vocabulary was from previous-year words and the error-spotting questions were short.

asked.q: Questions on the Five-Year Plans and the 1991 reforms (LPG).
A question on the 11th Schedule (Panchayat).
About 2 questions on space technology.
A statement-type question on the biosphere.
The idiom 'dark horse' (as recalled by candidates).
4–5 circle questions, plus triangles, trigonometry and mensuration.

observations: One centre reported a system shutdown during the paper, after which the timer resumed. Some candidates also reported mouse or PC hangs. These are centre-level reports.
A candidate survey (328 responses) reported an average of about 83 attempts and an average score near 133, and 61% of respondents called it more difficult than last year. The sample is self-selected.
disagreements: Overall difficulty: candidate interviews said easy to moderate or moderate, while the survey leaned difficult (61% difficult, 35% same, 4% easy).
General Awareness: reports about the polity and economy questions conflict, with some candidates recalling more of them than others.
Attempts: candidates claimed anywhere from 70 to 97 attempts, so there is no single good-attempts figure.

shifts.summary: Reviewers and candidates mostly called the evening paper moderate to difficult. Reasoning and English were easy to moderate, General Awareness was moderate and Quant was the toughest section. Quant leaned on advanced topics: mensuration (pyramid and prism), geometry and Data Interpretation with a histogram. A survey of 436 candidates found 48% calling it difficult, 45% choosing 'same' and 6% calling it easy. Good attempts were put at about 77–85, and the survey average of about 86 is self-reported and likely skews high. Opinions on General Awareness and Reasoning were split, and details are in the disagreements below.

sections.name: General Intelligence & Reasoning
sections.notes: Analytical reasoning had 7–8 questions. There were 2 coding-decoding, 2 syllogism and 3 matrix questions, plus 1 series, 1 figure-based and 1 roll-number question. No calendar or clock questions were reported. Candidates were split: some called it very easy and said 25 questions fit in 15 minutes, while others found it different from usual, with more statement and conclusion questions and fewer series questions.

sections.name: General Awareness
sections.notes: Reports differ: reviewers said only about 10–17 questions were comfortable, while some candidates called it easy and attempted 20–24. Candidates ranged from 'very easy' and 'easier than last year' to 'tough', with a couple of statement-based questions called hard. Economy had about 5 questions and polity about 3 to 4. Static GK was the main part. Current affairs was light: one candidate counted 3–4 questions from 2024–26, while a review said nothing from 2026 was asked. Candidates also recalled 2 to 3 folk-dance questions and 2 sports questions.

topics.topic: Polity: Article 61 (impeachment of the President), DPSP, Schedules
Art and culture: folk dances and instruments, monuments, architecture

sections.name: Quantitative Aptitude
sections.notes: Mensuration (3–5 questions, including pyramid, prism, sphere, hemisphere and cone) and geometry (3–4 questions, 1–2 on circles) had big shares. There were 4 algebra questions, 4 combining algebra and number system, and 1–2 polygon questions. Two time and work questions were lengthy. Data Interpretation had 2–4 questions. One histogram question was reported to have no diagram. One candidate said advanced maths made up about 60% of the section, and several candidates named Quant as the toughest section. The timer cut Quant attempts for many: candidates reported 18 to about 22 questions, and one said 6–7 questions could not be solved.

topics.topic: Mensuration: prism, pyramid, sphere, hemisphere, cone
Data Interpretation: pie chart, bar graph, histogram

sections.name: English Comprehension
sections.notes: Voice and narration had about 7–8 questions, which were lengthy rather than tough. There were 2 sentence-rearrangement (PQRS) questions and reading comprehension. Error-spotting was easy, and there was 1 sentence-improvement question. Vocabulary came from previous-year words, and one candidate called the cloze test hard to understand. Two candidates called the reading passage tough because of difficult words. Idioms and one-word substitution were also recalled.

asked.q: A question on the impeachment of the President (Article 61), as recalled by candidates.
A question on the full form of BIMSTEC.
A match-the-column question on the Schedules of the Constitution.
A question on the 2010 Commonwealth Games.
A question on census years (1991, 2001, 2011).
A question on which body issues the Global Innovation Index.
A question on the Deccan rivers.
A question on which scheme a small tailor can use to expand a business (PM Mudra Yojana), as recalled by reviewers.
Questions on the Air Chief Marshal during Operation Sindoor and on the chairman of the 16th Finance Commission, as recalled by reviewers.
A question on the origin state of the Dhimsa folk dance (Odisha), as recalled by candidates.
A question on the architectural style of the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (Victorian Gothic Revival), as recalled by reviewers.
A histogram question that, according to a candidate, came without the histogram diagram.
A pyramid question, recalled as a square base of area 81 sq cm and a slant height of 15 cm, asking for the vertical height.
Idiom questions on 'bury the hatchet' and 'go the whole hog', as recalled by one reviewer.

observations: SSC normalises scores across shifts, so a harder shift is expected to be balanced against easier ones.
Candidates in a Bareilly centre reported 3–4 system shutdowns during the paper, after which they logged in again and resumed. This is a centre-level report and not confirmed elsewhere.
Candidates who claimed 79–99 attempts also claimed about 90% accuracy. These are self-reported and the higher claims are doubtful.
Several candidates said the 15-minute sectional timer cost them Quant attempts, while Reasoning and General Awareness were hardly affected.
disagreements: Overall difficulty: an early survey of 121 responses had shown 55% 'same', 41% 'difficult' and 3% 'easy'. The larger survey of 436 responses now shows 48% 'difficult', 45% 'same' and 6% 'easy', which is much closer to the reviewers' moderate to difficult. Two of the reviews have near-identical figures and may not be independent.

General Awareness: candidates called it everything from very easy and easier than last year to tough. Reviewers' comfortable attempts were 13–17 in one review and 10–12 in another, while some candidates said they attempted 20–24.
Reasoning: some candidates called it very easy, while others found it different from the usual pattern, with more statement and conclusion questions.
Current affairs: one candidate counted 3–4 questions from 2024–26, while a review said nothing from 2026 was asked.

Survey averages: about 86 attempts and about 141 marks out of 200, which sit above the reviewers' good-attempts range. Self-selected survey samples tend to skew high. Individual candidates claimed 87 and 89 attempts.
Technical issues: one centre reported repeated shutdowns, while one review said mouse and keyboard problems were not seen at all.
Cut-off predictions on video reviews vary widely and are guesses, so none is reported here.

faqs.q: What was the difficulty level of SSC CGL 2026 Tier 1 on 5 October?
faqs.a: Shift 1 was reported as easy to moderate or moderate. Shift 2 was reported as easy to moderate or moderate, though a survey leaned difficult. Shift 3 was reported as moderate to difficult, with Quant the toughest section, and a survey of 436 candidates leaned the same way. All of this is unofficial.

faqs.q: How many good attempts were there on 5 October 2026?
faqs.a: For Shift 3 reviewers put it at about 77–85 out of 100, and a self-reported survey average was about 86. For Shifts 1 and 2 there is no reliable estimate, because individual candidates claimed anything from about 70 to 97 attempts. These are unofficial.

faqs.q: Which Quant topics were asked on 5 October?
faqs.a: Circles and other geometry, trigonometry, mensuration (prism, cone, pyramid, sphere, hemisphere), algebra, time and work and percentage-based arithmetic were reported. Data Interpretation was reported in Shift 3 but not in Shift 2.

faqs.q: Is the 15-minute sectional timer still in force?
faqs.a: Yes. Each section locks after 15 minutes and you cannot return to it, so skipping long questions early is important, especially in Quant.

faqs.q: Will a tougher shift lower my final score?
faqs.a: No. SSC normalises scores across shifts, so candidates in a harder shift are not penalised compared with those in an easier one.
